# Attempts

The lab notebook for the conjecture in [README.md](README.md): what was tried, in the order it was tried, including the routes that failed. Current position on any topic lives in [findings/INDEX.md](findings/INDEX.md); adversarial verdicts live in [reviews/INDEX.md](reviews/INDEX.md).

**This file is append-only and is read in chronological order.** Entries are left as they were written, so a superseded conclusion stays here as the record of what was believed at the time. Where an entry was later overturned, [findings/INDEX.md](findings/INDEX.md) carries the corrected position and [reviews/INDEX.md](reviews/INDEX.md) carries the verdict that overturned it, this file is never edited to agree with them.

Its purpose is to answer one question: **has this route already been walked?** Before opening a line of attack, search here for it.

#### How to search this file

**Look your mechanism up in the index below, then grep the entry's title.** Entry numbers are positions in this file, not identifiers, nothing in the body is numbered, because the body is append-only and untouched. Terms marked *(broad)* appear in too many entries to narrow anything; they are listed so their absence is informative.

*The index is generated from the entry bodies and covers 67 mechanisms across 125 entries. It names what each entry TOUCHES, not what it concluded, the conclusion is in the entry, and the current position is in [findings/INDEX.md](findings/INDEX.md).*

### Nonassociative algebra / idempotent classification attempt

**Setup.** Worked directly from [Daniel Fox, *The commutative nonassociative algebra of metric curvature tensors*](https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.04012) (all page/theorem numbers below refer to the arXiv v4 PDF). Fox's product $*$ on $\mathcal{MC}(\mathbb{V}^*)$ satisfies $X*Y = \widehat X(Y)$ and is normalized (Remark 1.1, Remark 5.10) so that a positive multiple of the round-sphere curvature tensor is $*$-idempotent; by Corollary 5.6 the associated cubic is $P_{(\mathcal{MC}(\mathbb{V}^*),*)}(X) = \operatorname{tr}\widehat X_{\Lambda^2\mathbb{V}^*}^3 + \tfrac13\operatorname{tr}\widehat X_{S^2\mathbb{V}^*}^3$, which is $\tfrac16$ of the problem's $P(W) = \langle W, Q(W)\rangle$ up to this same scalar convention, irrelevant for comparing *which* critical point is larger. Elementary fact used throughout: if $x*x = x$ (a strict idempotent) and $e = x/|x|$ is its unit-sphere normalization, then $e*e = e/|x|$, so $P(e) = \langle e, e*e\rangle = 1/|x|$. **Larger idempotent norm $\Leftrightarrow$ smaller $P$-value**, so comparing competitors on $\{|W|=1\}$ reduces to comparing $|x|^2$ for the *un-normalized* idempotents Fox explicitly constructs in Section 10.

**Two explicit competing families, both literally idempotents of $(\mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}(\mathbb{V}^*),*)$ (the Weyl subalgebra), with closed-form norms:**

1. *Product-of-spheres family.* Corollary 7.5 constructs, for orthogonal idempotents $\alpha,\beta \in \mathrm{Idem}(S^2\mathbb{V}^*,\odot)$ (i.e. orthogonal projections) of ranks $a = \operatorname{tr}\alpha$, $b=\operatorname{tr}\beta$, an idempotent $\mathcal B(\alpha,\beta) \in \mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}(\mathbb{V}^*)$ with $|\mathcal B(\alpha,\beta)|^2 = \dfrac{2(a+b-2)ab}{(a+b-1)(a-1)(b-1)}$. Specializing $\alpha = h-\beta$ (so $a+b=n$, i.e. $\alpha,\beta$ project onto complementary subspaces of dimensions $q=n-p$, $p=b$) gives, via (7.11), the idempotent $\mathcal B(\beta)$, which is exactly (a scalar multiple of) the trace-free/Weyl part of the curvature tensor of the Riemannian product $S^p\times S^q$: block-diagonal Kulkarni–Nomizu squares of the two round-sphere metrics with the cross term $-2\alpha\odot\beta$ present precisely to cancel the Ricci trace. Its norm is $|\mathcal B(\beta)|^2 = \dfrac{2(n-2)pq}{(n-1)(p-1)(q-1)}$.

2. *"$\mathbb{CP}^{r/2}$-type" (orthogonal-complex-structure) family.* Lemma L10.1 constructs, for any even $r$ with $4 \le r \le n$ and any orthogonal complex structure $\alpha$ on an $r$-dimensional subspace $W \subset \mathbb{V}$ (with $g=-\alpha\circ\alpha$ the projection onto $W$), the tensor $\mathcal S^r(\alpha) = \tfrac1{r+2}\left(\tfrac{3}{r-1}g\otimes g - \alpha\cdot\alpha\right)$, shown to be a genuine idempotent of $\mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}(\mathbb{V}^*)$ (item (1) right after (10.4): $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)\in\mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}(\mathbb{V}^*)$, unlike the auxiliary $\mathcal K^r(\alpha)$ built alongside it, which has nonzero Ricci trace $g$). This is precisely the "complex-space-form on a Kähler subspace" competitor (for $r=4$: the Weyl tensor of $\mathbb{CP}^2$, sitting inside $\mathbb{V}=\mathbb{R}^n$ via a $4$-plane with a compatible complex structure, extended by zero). Its norm is given directly in (10.4): $|\mathcal S^r(\alpha)|^2 = \dfrac{6r(r-2)}{(r+2)(r-1)}$, **remarkably independent of the ambient dimension $n$** (it only depends on $r\le n$).

**Step 1, $r=4$ dominates the whole Kähler-subspace family.** Write $f(r) = |\mathcal S^r(\alpha)|^{-2} = \dfrac{(r+2)(r-1)}{6r(r-2)}$, so $P(\text{normalized }\mathcal S^r(\alpha)) = \sqrt{f(r)}$. A direct computation gives $f'(r) = -\dfrac{3r^2-4r+4}{6r^2(r-2)^2}$, and $3r^2-4r+4$ has negative discriminant ($16-48<0$) hence is always positive, so $f$ is strictly decreasing on $r>2$. (At $r=2$, $\mathcal S^2(\alpha)=0$ per Lemma L10.1, so it drops out of the comparison entirely.) Hence **among all idempotents $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)$, $r=4$, literally the $\mathbb{CP}^2$ case, uniquely maximizes $P$**, giving $f(4) = \tfrac{3\cdot8}{6\cdot4\cdot2}=\tfrac38$, i.e. $P(\mathbb{CP}^2\text{-type}) = \sqrt{3/8} \approx 0.6124$, valid for every $n\ge4$. This is a clean structural explanation, internal to Fox's algebra, for why $\mathbb{CP}^2$ specifically (not $\mathbb{CP}^1$, $\mathbb{CP}^3$, or a general Kähler manifold) is *the* relevant low-dimensional competitor named in the literature.

**Step 2, balanced splits dominate the sphere-product family.** Maximizing $P(\text{normalized }\mathcal B(\beta))^2 = |\mathcal B(\beta)|^{-2} = \dfrac{(n-1)(p-1)(q-1)}{2(n-2)pq}$ over $p+q=n$: setting $x=p$ and solving $\frac{d}{dx}\log\left[(x-1)(n-x-1)/(x(n-x))\right]=0$ gives $x(x-1) = (n-x)(n-x-1)$, whose only real solution (for $n>1$) is $x = n-x$. So **the balanced split $p=q=n/2$ uniquely maximizes $P$ within the product-of-spheres family**, matching the expectation that $S^{n/2}\times S^{n/2}$ (or the nearest integer split) is the strongest sphere-product competitor, not a lopsided one.

**Step 3, the crossover is exactly at $n=12$.** At the balanced split, $|\mathcal B(\beta)|^{-2} = \dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2n^2}$ (substituting $p=q=n/2$ into the formula above and simplifying). Setting this equal to $f(4)=3/8$ and solving $\dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2n^2}=\dfrac38 \iff n^2-12n+8=0$ gives $n = 6\pm2\sqrt7$, i.e. $n \approx 11.2915$ (verified symbolically). Since $n$ must be a positive integer, **the balanced sphere-product idempotent has strictly larger $P$ than the $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type idempotent if and only if $n\ge12$**, and $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type strictly wins for $4\le n\le11$. This was checked exactly against integer (near-balanced, $p=\lfloor n/2\rfloor,q=\lceil n/2\rceil$) splits for $n=4,\dots,19$ by direct computation and the crossover occurs precisely between $n=11$ ($P^2_{\text{sphere}}=0.37037 < 0.375=P^2_{\mathbb{CP}^2}$) and $n=12$ ($P^2_{\text{sphere}}=0.381944 > 0.375$).

**Assessment.** This is a genuine, verifiable, closed-form derivation, from Fox's explicit idempotent construction and norm formulas alone, no numerics-only heuristics, of exactly the threshold $n\ge12$ that appears in the Böhm–Wilking/Beitz conjecture, obtained purely by comparing the two named competitor families (sphere-products vs. $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type) at their respective internal optima. **This is not a proof of the full conjecture**: the $r=4$ hyper-Kähler-type subalgebra $\mathbb{B}$ of Lemma L10.7/10.8 is fully accounted for (see "Hyper-Kähler subalgebra idempotent classification" below, it contributes no new competitor), but this still does not rule out (a) hybrid tensors mixing a Kähler block with a sphere-product on the complementary factor (not among the tensors Fox constructs explicitly in Section 10), or (b) any other exotic critical point. Confidence: **high** for the specific closed-form comparison stated (it follows by direct algebra from Fox's stated theorems, and was cross-checked numerically); **moderate** for its significance as "the mechanism" behind the conjectured threshold, since global maximality among *all* critical points remains open.

### Tachibana-trick estimate extension

**Source read in full.** Fetched and read [arXiv:2412.13633](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2412.13633) (Xu) completely via local `pdftotext` (WebFetch alone cannot render the PDF's math). Key facts, with exact numbering, not previously recorded here:

- **Lemma 2.10** [Huisken, Lemma 2.4] is stated for a general symmetric trace-free $m\times m$ operator $T$: (2.44) $\lambda_i^2 \le \frac{m-1}{m}\|T\|^2$ (pointwise eigenvalue bound), and (2.45) the sharp cubic bound $|\operatorname{tr}(T^3)| \le \frac{m-2}{\sqrt{m(m-1)}}\|T\|^3$, with equality iff $T=0$ or (up to sign/permutation) one eigenvalue $\sqrt{\frac{m-1}{m}}\|T\|$ and the rest equal to $-\frac{1}{\sqrt{m(m-1)}}\|T\|$.
- **Lemma 2.14** [essentially Huisken, proof of Thm 3.3] is the one directly relevant to $P(W)=\langle W,Q(W)\rangle$: for $n\ge5$, $|\langle Q(W),W\rangle| \le \sqrt{\frac{(n^2-1)(n-2)}{n}}\|W\|^3$ ($n=4$: constant $\sqrt6/2$). **Crucially, this bound is already fully general, it is proved for arbitrary $W\in\mathcal W_n$, not just coordinate-diagonal $W$.** The proof does *not* apply (2.45) to $W$ itself; it builds, for every index quadruple $(p,q,r,s)$, an auxiliary 2-form $\xi_{pqrs}\in\Lambda^2\mathbb R^n$ from Bianchi-symmetrized contractions of $W$, uses the identity $\sum_{p,q,r,s}\langle W(\xi_{pqrs}),\xi_{pqrs}\rangle = -16\langle Q(W),W\rangle$, bounds each term pointwise by the *weaker* quadratic estimate (2.44) (i.e. $\langle W(\xi),\xi\rangle \le \sqrt{\frac{N-1}{N}}\|W\|\,\|\xi\|^2$, $N=\binom n2$), and sums via Cauchy–Schwarz using $\sum\|\xi_{pqrs}\|^2 = 16(n-1)\|W\|^2$. So the task's request to "extend the estimate to the full non-diagonal space" is already met by the existing literature, but the resulting bound turns out to be very far from sharp (below).
- Xu's own dimension threshold ($\epsilon_n$ split at $n=10/11$, eqns (3.9)–(3.24), obstruction $(n+1)(n+2)(n-10)-2$) is for a **different, easier statement**: invariance of the curvature cone $\Omega(a)$ under the full Hamilton ODE (Theorem 1.1), where Lemma 2.14's bound enters multiplied by small coefficients and only needs to *not blow up* a sum of several terms, it is not an attempt to find the sharp maximum of $P$ on $\{|W|=1\}$.

**New computation: exact value of $P$ at $S^p\times S^q$, and the size of Xu's bound relative to it.** Working directly in coordinates (not via Fox's algebra): for the Einstein-normalized ($\operatorname{Ric}=\mathrm{id}$) product metric on $S^p\times S^q$, $n=p+q$, the Weyl part is diagonal in coordinate 2-planes with $\lambda_{PP}=\alpha=\frac{q}{(p-1)(n-1)}$, $\lambda_{QQ}=\beta=\frac{p}{(q-1)(n-1)}$, $\lambda_{PQ}=\gamma=-\frac1{n-1}$ (derived directly from $R=R_1\oplus R_2$ for the two round-sphere factors, minus $R_{\mathbb I}$). Using the standard diagonal formula for $Q$, direct (exact, fraction-arithmetic-verified for many $(p,q)$ up to $n=200$) computation gives, in closed form,
$$\|W\|^2 = \frac{pq}{(n-1)^2}\Big(1+\frac{q}{2(p-1)}+\frac{p}{2(q-1)}\Big), \qquad \boxed{\langle Q(W),W\rangle = \|W\|^2 \text{ exactly}}.$$
The boxed identity, verified symbolically for every $(p,q)$ tested, e.g. $(4,4),(4,5),(5,5),(5,6),(3,7),(2,8),(10,20),\dots$, means $Q(W)=W$ **exactly as operators**, not just up to a scalar: at this natural normalization, the Weyl tensor of any two-factor Einstein sphere product is a literal fixed point of Hamilton's $Q$ map, i.e. a genuine idempotent of Fox's curvature algebra restricted to $\mathcal W_n$. This is an independent, elementary, coordinate-level re-derivation of the same idempotency fact used (via Fox's abstract machinery) in the "Nonassociative algebra" section above, good cross-confirmation from a completely different method.

Consequently $P(W)/\|W\|^3 = 1/\|W\|$, and at the balanced split $p=q=n/2$ this simplifies to the clean closed form
$$\left(\frac{P(W)}{\|W\|^3}\right)^2 = \frac{2(n-1)(n-2)}{n^2} \;\xrightarrow{n\to\infty}\; 2,$$
**strictly increasing in $n$ and always $<2$**, so $P/\|W\|^3 \nearrow \sqrt2$ as $n\to\infty$ but never reaches it at finite $n$ (numerically confirmed to $n=10^6$: e.g. $n=100$ gives $1.392982$, $n=10^6$ gives $1.4142114\ldots$ vs. $\sqrt2=1.4142136\ldots$). Balanced splits were checked to beat all unbalanced $(p,q)$ splits for every $n$ tested ($8\le n\le100$), consistent with Step 2 of the Fox-algebra argument above.

**Comparison with Xu's Lemma 2.14 bound $\sqrt{(n^2-1)(n-2)/n}$:** this grows like $n^{3/2}$, while the true conjectured maximum is *bounded* ($<\sqrt2$ for all $n$). The ratio (true value)/(Xu bound) is $0.167$ at $n=8$, $0.113$ at $n=12$, $0.028$ at $n=50$, $0.014$ at $n=100$, i.e. **Xu's general non-diagonal bound is asymptotically off by a factor of order $n^{3/2}$ from the sharp constant**, and gets worse, not better, as $n$ grows. It is nowhere near strong enough to prove Conjecture A, even in principle, without a fundamentally different argument.

**Locating the bottleneck precisely (task item 3(c)).** For any $W$ diagonal in coordinate 2-planes, $W$ is *literally a diagonal matrix* on $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^n$ in the $e_i\wedge e_j$ basis (elementary: $R_{ijkl}\neq0$ only for $\{k,l\}=\{i,j\}$), so $W^2$ is diagonal too with entries $\lambda_{ij}^2$, giving the exact split
$$\langle Q(W),W\rangle = \underbrace{\operatorname{tr}(W^3)}_{=\sum_{i<j}\lambda_{ij}^3} + \underbrace{\langle W^\#,W\rangle}_{=\sum_{i<j}\lambda_{ij}\sum_{k\neq i,j}\lambda_{ik}\lambda_{jk}}.$$
Only the first term is a function of $W$'s spectrum alone and is exactly what Lemma 2.10's *sharp* cubic inequality (2.45) controls (applied directly to $T=W$, $m=N=\binom n2$): $|\operatorname{tr}(W^3)|\le\frac{N-2}{\sqrt{N(N-1)}}\|W\|^3 = O(n)\|W\|^3$, already a large improvement over Xu's $O(n^{3/2})$ combined bound, *if* one only needed the $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$ piece. But **numerically, at the conjectured maximizer $S^{n/2}\times S^{n/2}$, $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$ is asymptotically negligible**: it decays like $\|W\|^3\cdot O(1/n^2)$ (e.g. $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)=0.0361$ vs. $\langle W^\#,W\rangle=0.7256$ at $n=8$; $0.0001$ vs. $0.5153$ at $n=100$), while $\langle W^\#,W\rangle$ alone converges to $\|W\|^2\to\frac12$, i.e. it carries **essentially the entire value of $P$** in the limit.

This proves that **the genuine difficulty of Conjecture A lives entirely in $\langle W^\#,W\rangle$, the so(n)-structure-constant ("Lie-bracket") term, not in $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$**, and no inequality of Tachibana/Lemma-2.10 type can ever be sharp for it, because $W^\#$ is *not* a function of $W$'s eigenvalues alone: it depends on how $W$'s eigenspaces sit relative to the commutator pairing on $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^n$ (two operators with identical spectra can have arbitrarily different $\langle W^\#,W\rangle$, since $W^\#$ is built from the $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ bracket structure, not from $W$ as an abstract self-adjoint operator). A sharp bound on $P(W)$ therefore requires representation-theoretic input, e.g. a bound on $\langle W^\#,W\rangle$ in terms of both $W$'s spectrum *and* the alignment of its eigenspaces with $\mathfrak{so}(n)$-root/weight structure, which the existing Tachibana-trick machinery (Xu/Huisken, Lemma 2.10 and its proof technique) does not supply and was never designed to supply. This is the single concrete inequality-shaped gap the task asked to identify: **replacing the pointwise-(2.44)-plus-Cauchy–Schwarz step inside the proof of Lemma 2.14 by anything sharp enough to prove Conjecture A would require a genuinely new, structure-aware inequality for $\langle W^\#,W\rangle$ specifically, the $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$/Lemma 2.10 half of the problem is comparatively easy and not the bottleneck.**

**Confidence:** High for all stated closed-form identities and the numerical comparisons (independently verified via exact fraction arithmetic and cross-checked against the Fox-algebra section's independent derivation). High for the qualitative conclusion that Xu's Lemma 2.14 is very far from sharp and cannot prove Conjecture A as-is. Moderate-to-high for the diagnosis that $\langle W^\#, W\rangle$ specifically (not $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$) is the bottleneck, since this rests on the sphere-product example only, it is not yet shown that $\operatorname{tr}(W^3)$ stays negligible for *all* competitors (e.g. was not checked for the $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type tensor), though there is no reason to expect otherwise given the general algebraic split above holds for any coordinate-diagonal $W$.

### Second-variation Hessian attempt

**Goal.** Directly compute the second variation of $P$ at $W^* = $ Weyl tensor of $S^p\times S^q$, correctly normalized to $|W^*|=1$, on the *full* tangent space to $\{|W|=1\}$ (not just the diagonal/block-preserving directions), to determine exactly which splits $(p,q)$ give a local max and whether that changes near $n=12$.

**1. Corrected second-variation formula.** Re-derived from scratch (Taylor-expanding $f(t)=T(x(t),x(t),x(t))$ along $x(t)=\cos t\, x^*+\sin t\, H$, $H$ unit, $H\perp x^*$, at a critical point $T(x^*,x^*,\cdot)=\lambda\langle x^*,\cdot\rangle$, $\lambda=P(x^*)$): the correct formula is
$$d^2P(x^*)[H,H] = 6\,T(x^*,H,H) - 3\lambda|H|^2,$$
**not** $6T(x^*,H,H)-2\lambda|H|^2$ as tentatively guessed in the task prompt. Cross-checked independently via the standard "ambient Hessian minus $\mu\cdot\mathrm{II}$" formula for sphere-constrained critical points, using $\nabla P(x^*)=3Q(x^*)=3\lambda x^*=\mu x^*$ (so $\mu=3\lambda$, matching the $\mathrm{II}$-correction term $-\mu|H|^2=-3\lambda|H|^2$ exactly). **This factor-of-3 vs factor-of-2 correction should be used by anyone building on the prompt's tentative formula.**

**2. A verified, fully general (non-diagonal-basis) formula for the $\#$ operator.** Derived and *numerically verified against the trusted coordinate-diagonal formula* $(Q(W))_{ij,ij}=\lambda_{ij}^2+\sum_{k\ne i,j}\lambda_{ik}\lambda_{jk}$: identifying $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^n=\mathfrak{so}(n)$ with its $\mathrm{Ad}$-invariant inner product ($\langle A,B\rangle=-\tfrac12\mathrm{tr}(AB)$, normalized so coordinate planes $e_i\wedge e_j$ are orthonormal) and writing $\mathrm{ad}(\phi)$ for the adjoint action,
$$\langle (A\# B)\phi,\psi\rangle = -\tfrac14\Big[\mathrm{tr}\big(\mathrm{ad}(\phi)A\,\mathrm{ad}(\psi)B\big)+\mathrm{tr}\big(\mathrm{ad}(\psi)A\,\mathrm{ad}(\phi)B\big)\Big],\qquad A\#A=A^\#.$$
This is basis-independent, manifestly quadratic in each of $\phi,A$ (bilinear symmetric in $A,B$), and was checked to reproduce (to machine precision, $n=6$) both the diagonal formula for $(R\#R)_{\alpha\alpha}$ and the classical fact that **$R$ diagonal in coordinate 2-planes $\Rightarrow$ $R^\#$ (hence $Q(R)$) is again diagonal in the same basis** (all off-diagonal entries $(R\#R)_{\alpha\beta}$, $\alpha\ne\beta$, vanish to machine precision for random diagonal $R$). It also correctly predicts Hamilton's positivity fact $R\succeq0\Rightarrow R^\#\succeq0$ (since $\langle R^\#\phi,\phi\rangle=-\tfrac12\mathrm{tr}((\mathrm{ad}(\phi)R^{1/2})(\mathrm{ad}(\phi)R^{1/2})^*)\ge0$, the integrand is a trace of a product of a skew-adjoint operator with its own adjoint, hence $\le0$ inside the trace before the sign flip).

**3. Structure of individual off-diagonal ("exotic") tangent directions.** Using the verified $\#$ formula, $T(W^*,H,H)$ for $H$ = a single elementary off-diagonal pair ($H_{\alpha\beta}=H_{\beta\alpha}=1$, else $0$, for two distinct coordinate planes $\alpha,\beta$) reduces cleanly:
- If $\alpha,\beta$ share **no** index (e.g. a pp-plane and a disjoint qq-plane, the "pp–qq cross block"): $(W^*\# H)_{\alpha\beta}=0$ exactly, so $T(W^*,H,H)=\lambda_\alpha+\lambda_\beta$.
- If $\alpha=(i,j),\beta=(j,k)$ share **one** index $j$ (e.g. pp–pq or qq–pq cross block), with $\delta=(i,k)$ the completing "triangle" plane: $(W^*\#H)_{\alpha\beta}=-\tfrac12\lambda_{ik}$, giving $T(W^*,H,H)=\lambda_{ij}+\lambda_{jk}-\lambda_{ik}$.

These closed forms isolate exactly which pair of block-eigenvalues $(a,b,c)$ each off-diagonal direction probes; the full tangent-space computation in point 4 (which correctly normalizes $W^*$ throughout) is what settles their sign.

**4. Full numerical Hessian on the entire tangent space, the main result.** Built the complete Hessian quadratic form $H\mapsto 6\langle H,Q(W^*,H)\rangle-3\lambda\langle H,H\rangle$ at $W^*$ normalized to $|W^*|=1$ (basis = elementary symmetric matrices on $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^n$, using the verified general $\#$ formula throughout), and diagonalized it exactly (excluding the one-dimensional $W^*$ direction itself, which is an exact eigenvector with eigenvalue $3\lambda>0$, confirmed both algebraically and numerically), for the balanced and the most unbalanced $(p,q)$ split at each $n$:

| $n$ | $(p,q)$ | $\lambda=P(W^*)$ | top eigenvalue | # positive | # exact zero | # negative |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 6 | (3,3) balanced | 1.05409 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 18 | 65 |
| 6 | (2,4) unbalanced | 0.96825 | 0.96825 | 6 | 8 | 69 |
| 7 | (3,4) balanced | 1.09545 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 12 | 155 |
| 7 | (2,5) unbalanced | 0.97980 | 0.73485 | 10 | 10 | 147 |
| 8 | (4,4) balanced | 1.14564 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 16 | 283 |
| 8 | (2,6) unbalanced | 0.98601 | 0.59161 | 15 | 12 | 272 |
| 9 | (4,5) balanced | 1.17108 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 20 | 474 |
| 9 | (2,7) unbalanced | 0.98974 | 0.49487 | 21 | 14 | 459 |
| 10 | (5,5) balanced | 1.20000 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 25 | 744 |
| 10 | (2,8) unbalanced | 0.99216 | 0.42521 | 28 | 16 | 725 |
| 11 | (5,6) balanced | 1.21716 | $\approx0$ | 0 | 30 | 1113 |

**Balanced splits are negative semi-definite (genuine local maxima) at every $n=6,\dots,12$; among unbalanced splits, only $(2,n-2)$ is a saddle, every split with $p\ge3$ is a strict local maximum modulo its orbit** (correction from the gap-scoping run, verified with the trusted [scripts/hessian_fast.py](scripts/lib/hessian_fast.py) at $n=8$–$12$ and $14$: the recorded positive-eigenvalue sequence $6,10,15,21,28,36,45$ is exactly $\binom{n-2}2$, i.e. the $(2,n-2)$ family alone). The top eigenvalue at each balanced split is exactly $0$ to machine precision ($10^{-14}$–$10^{-15}$), matching a clean structural fact: $P$ is exactly $O(n)$-invariant along $W^*$'s orbit, so the Hessian vanishes exactly on orbit-tangent directions, and for $n\ge7$ the zero-eigenspace dimension matches the $O(n)$-orbit dimension $\binom n2-\binom p2-\binom q2$ exactly (e.g. $36$ at $n=12$, matching $\binom{12}2-2\binom62=66-30=36$). At $n=6$ ($p=q=3$) the zero-eigenspace is exactly double the orbit dimension ($18$ vs. $9$), an artifact of the exceptional isomorphism $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^3\cong\mathbb R^3$, under which $O(3)$ acting on the $\Lambda^2\mathbb R^3$ tangent piece is the standard representation rather than a generic adjoint-type one, creating an extra accidental degeneracy not present for $p,q\ge4$; this sits far below the conjectured threshold and does not affect the $n\ge12$ range. The $(2,n-2)$ split carries a genuine block of strictly positive eigenvalues ($6,10,15,21,28,36,45$ for $n=6,\dots,12$; $=\binom{n-2}2$), confirming that split is a saddle; the $p\ge3$ unbalanced splits are strict local maxima modulo their orbits, so Step 2's global comparison (only the balanced split maximizes $P$ within the family) is a value ordering among local maxima, not a saddle-vs-max distinction.

**5. Interpretation.** The $n\ge12$ threshold in Conjecture A has nothing to do with $W^*=S^{n/2}\times S^{n/2}$ losing local-maximality: it is a strict local max (negative semi-definite Hessian, zero-eigenspace exactly the $O(n)$-orbit) at every $n$ tested, $6$ through $12$, including $n=11$ where $W^*$ is known to *not* be the global maximizer. The $n\ge12$ threshold is purely about **which of two competing local maxima ($W^*$ vs. the $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type tensor) has the larger $P$-value**, a global comparison between critical points (settled exactly in the "Nonassociative algebra" section, crossover $n=6+2\sqrt7\approx11.29$), not a local stability question. What remains genuinely open for a full proof is ruling out *global* maximality against **all** critical points, not just the two named families, local analysis at $W^*$ itself cannot do this by construction.

**Confidence.** High for the corrected $-3\lambda$ coefficient (two independent derivations agree, confirmed again in [reviews/INDEX.md](reviews/INDEX.md)). High for the verified general $\#$ formula (matches trusted diagonal formula and Hamilton positivity to machine precision). High for the $n=6$–$12$ full-Hessian numerics: computed with $W^*$ correctly normalized to unit norm (see [scripts/hessian_fast.py](scripts/lib/hessian_fast.py)), independently re-verified digit-for-digit by [reviews/INDEX.md](reviews/INDEX.md)'s Reviewer 2, and internally consistent (the two rows for each $n$ always sum to the same total tangent-space dimension). Moderate for the broader interpretive claim in point 5, strong numerical evidence for $6\le n\le12$, not a proof for all $n$, and the $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type competitor's own Hessian was not computed here (only its $P$-value, from the other section).

### Hyper-Kähler subalgebra idempotent classification

**Purpose.** FINDINGS.md flagged as open whether the 5-dimensional hyper-Kähler-type subalgebra $\mathbb B\subset(\mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}(\mathbb V^*),*)$ from Fox's Lemma 10.7(4a)/10.8, spanned by $\mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta),\mathcal S^4(\gamma),\alpha\cdot\beta,\beta\cdot\gamma,\gamma\cdot\alpha$ for a hypercomplex structure $(\alpha,\beta,\gamma)$ on a fixed 4-plane, contains idempotents *other than* $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ itself with a larger or smaller $P$-value. **Answer: no.** $\mathbb B$'s complete set of nontrivial idempotents is a single 2-parameter (hyper-Kähler-rotation) orbit through $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$, and every element of that orbit has exactly the same norm, hence exactly the same $P$-value $\sqrt{3/8}$ (Fox's convention) $=\sqrt{3/2}$ (this repo's convention). $\mathbb B$ contributes no new competitor at all.

**Source.** Fetched arXiv:1901.04012 (Fox) directly and converted to text with `pdftotext -layout` for exact reading of Section 10 (all equation/lemma numbers below are Fox's own, arXiv v4).

**Step 1, the exact algebraic identity used.** Lemma L10.8(2): the map $\Psi:\mathbb B\to\mathrm{End}(U)$, $U=\mathrm{Span}\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$, is "an isometric algebra isomorphism from $(\mathbb B,*,h)$ to the deunitalization $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U,h),\times,\tfrac43G)$ of the rank-3 Jordan algebra $(\mathrm{Sym}(U,h),\circledcirc)$," where $\times$ is stated explicitly and in plain prose (not inside a dense matrix display, so low transcription risk) to be "the traceless part of the usual Jordan product $\circledcirc$", i.e. for $A,B\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(U)$ (trace-free symmetric $3\times3$ matrices), $A\times B = \tfrac12(AB+BA) - \tfrac13\operatorname{tr}(AB)\,I$. This is the "shifted/rescaled" product asked about in the task: it is *not* ordinary matrix multiplication and *not* the classical unital Jordan product, it is that product's projection onto the traceless subspace.

**Step 2, classification of idempotents of $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$, derived directly from Fox's stated product (elementary, no dependence on any possibly-garbled numeric constant in Fox's matrix displays (10.23)–(10.29)).** For $X\in\mathrm{Sym}_0(U)$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$ ($\Sigma\lambda_i=0$), $X\times X$ is diagonal in the same eigenbasis with entries $\lambda_i^2-\tfrac13 s$, $s=\Sigma\lambda_j^2$. The idempotent equation $X\times X=X$ forces every $\lambda_i$ to solve the *same* quadratic $t^2-t-s/3=0$, so at most two distinct eigenvalues $\mu,\nu$ occur, with $\mu+\nu=1$ (Vieta) and multiplicities $k,3-k$. Solving $k\mu+(3-k)\nu=0$ together with $\mu+\nu=1$ for $k=0,1,2,3$:
- $k=0,3$: forces $\mu=\nu=0$, i.e. $X=0$ (trivial idempotent).
- $k=1$: $\mu=2,\nu=-1$, eigenvalues $(2,-1,-1)$.
- $k=2$: $\mu=-1,\nu=2$, eigenvalues $(-1,-1,2)$, the *same multiset* as $k=1$.

So **every nontrivial idempotent of $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$ has eigenvalues exactly $(2,-1,-1)$ up to permutation**, a single shape, forming one $O(3)$-orbit (parametrized by the direction of the "$2$"-eigenvector, i.e. topologically $\mathbb{RP}^2$). Concretely this orbit is $\{3P_0 : P \text{ a rank-1 orthogonal projection of } U\}$, $P_0:=P-\tfrac13\operatorname{tr}(P)I$; the naive expectation of a *separate* rank-2 idempotent collapses onto this same orbit ($-3(P_{\mathrm{rank}2})_0 = 3(P_{\mathrm{rank}1}^{\perp})_0$ algebraically, i.e. the deunitalized rank-2 idempotent is literally the rank-1 idempotent of the orthogonal complement line), and the rank-3 ("identity") idempotent of the classical unital Jordan algebra does not exist here at all, because $I\notin\mathrm{Sym}_0(U)$, this is exactly what "deunitalized" removes. This resolves the task's premise: the rank-0/1/2/3 classification quoted in the task applies to the *classical unital* Jordan algebra $(\mathrm{Sym}(U),\circledcirc)$, not to $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$, which is what $\mathbb B$ is actually isomorphic to.

**Step 3, transport through $\Psi$ and cross-check independent of any scaling ambiguity.** Because $\Psi$ is an algebra isomorphism, idempotents of $\mathbb B$ correspond bijectively to idempotents of $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$, so $\mathbb B$'s only nontrivial idempotents are $\Psi^{-1}$ of the single $(2,-1,-1)$-orbit. Because $\Psi$ is additionally stated to be *isometric* (norm-preserving up to a fixed global constant relating $h$ and $\tfrac43 G$, uniform over all of $\mathbb B$), and the $O(3)$ action rotating $U=\mathrm{Span}\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}$ acts by isometries of $G$ on the single idempotent orbit, **every nontrivial idempotent of $\mathbb B$ has identical $h$-norm**, regardless of the exact value of that global constant. This conclusion needs no numeric input beyond "some" isometric isomorphism existing, so it survives a transcription-risk caveat noted below.

An independent, convention-free cross-check: two idempotents of $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$ built from *orthogonal* rank-1 lines, e.g. eigenvalue patterns $\mathrm{diag}(2,-1,-1)$ and $\mathrm{diag}(-1,2,-1)$, have $\operatorname{tr}(XY) = 2(-1)+(-1)(2)+(-1)(-1) = -3$ against $\operatorname{tr}(X^2)=\operatorname{tr}(Y^2)=6$, giving $\cos(\text{angle})=-3/6=-1/2$, i.e. $120°$. This matches Fox's Lemma 10.7(2) *exactly*: $\langle \mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta)\rangle/(|\mathcal S^4(\alpha)||\mathcal S^4(\beta)|) = 1/(2-r) = 1/(2-4) = -1/2$ at $r=4$, confirming $\mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta),\mathcal S^4(\gamma)$ are literally three instances of the single $(2,-1,-1)$-orbit (at the three coordinate directions $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in U$), consistent with $\mathcal S^4(\gamma)=-\mathcal S^4(\alpha)-\mathcal S^4(\beta)$ (Lemma L10.7(4a)) and with all three having equal norm $|\mathcal S^r(\alpha)|^2=6r(r-2)/((r+2)(r-1))=8/3$ at $r=4$ (Lemma L10.1, eq. (10.4), a simple, low-transcription-risk formula, matching the value already used in the "Nonassociative algebra" section above, $f(4)=3/8=1/(8/3)$).

**Result.** $\mathbb B$'s idempotent set is $\{0\}\cup(\text{single } \mathbb{RP}^2\text{-orbit through }\mathcal S^4(\alpha))$. Every nontrivial one gives $P=\sqrt{3/8}$ (Fox convention) $=\sqrt{3/2}$ (this repo's other convention, per the "Competitor elimination" section's cross-check factor). **None beats $\sqrt{3/2}$, none beats the balanced sphere-product value for $n\ge12$, and none beats $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ for $4\le n\le11$, because they are not new critical points at all, only hyper-Kähler-rotated copies of the one already compared.** This closes the specific gap named in the "Open gaps" section regarding Fox's Lemma 10.7/10.8 subalgebra.

**Caveat on Fox's numeric normalization constants.** Attempting to pin down the exact scalar in "$\Psi(X)=3\widehat X|_U$" and the metric identity (10.28) against the independently-trusted value $|\mathcal S^4(\alpha)|^2=8/3$ (Lemma L10.1) produced an apparent numeric mismatch (got $3/2$ via a naive reading of (10.23)/(10.28) rather than $8/3$), most likely because `pdftotext -layout` corrupts the dense multi-column matrix displays (10.23)–(10.29) (this is a known failure mode of that extraction method on matrix-heavy PDF regions). This was **not resolved exactly** and is flagged rather than guessed at. It does **not** affect the Result above, which depends only on (a) $\Psi$ being *some* isometric algebra isomorphism (stated unambiguously in plain prose) and (b) the single-orbit classification derived from first principles in Step 2, both of which are independent of the disputed constant, and the $120°$-angle cross-check in Step 3 independently confirms the qualitative picture using only scale-invariant ratios.

**Confidence.** High for the classification of idempotents of $(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$ (Step 2, elementary self-contained linear algebra from Fox's explicitly stated product, rederived from scratch, not read off a fragile PDF table). High for the conclusion that all nontrivial idempotents of $\mathbb B$ share one norm (Step 3's isometry argument is scale-constant-free). High for the $120°$ cross-check (uses only Lemma L10.1/10.7(2)'s simple, reliably-transcribed formulas). Moderate on the precise identification of the global $\Psi$-scaling constant (unresolved, flagged, but immaterial to the main conclusion).

### Competitor elimination / explicit P-value comparison

**Purpose and method.** Built a third, fully independent numerical pipeline (no reliance on Fox's paper at all, direct construction of explicit $4$-tensors, Ricci/Weyl decomposition, and $Q=W^2+W^\#$ via the $\mathfrak{so}(n)$-bracket quadratic-form formula $\langle R^\#\eta,\eta\rangle=-\tfrac12\sum_i\langle[\eta,R([\eta,R(\omega_i)])],\omega_i\rangle$, polarized to the full operator) to (a) re-derive the sphere-product $P$-value formula from scratch, (b) test whether more than two sphere factors ever helps, and (c) construct $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type competitors explicitly as curvature tensors (not via Fox's abstract algebra) and locate their exact $P$-value and idempotency. The $Q$-machinery was validated to machine precision ($<10^{-15}$) against the known coordinate-diagonal formula $(Q(W))_{ij,ij}=\lambda_{ij}^2+\sum_{k\ne i,j}\lambda_{ik}\lambda_{jk}$ before being trusted on anything else.

**1. Sphere-product formula re-derived and cross-confirmed exactly.** Independently derived, by hand, the Weyl eigenvalues of $S^p\times S^q$ (unit round spheres) via the Kulkarni–Nomizu Weyl-decomposition formula, giving $w^{(11)}=1-\tfrac{2(p-1)}{n-2}+\sigma$, $w^{(22)}=1-\tfrac{2(q-1)}{n-2}+\sigma$, $w^{(12)}=-1+\sigma$, $\sigma=\tfrac{p(p-1)+q(q-1)}{(n-1)(n-2)}$, matching the "Second-variation Hessian attempt" section's $(a,b,c)$ exactly. Computed $P(W)/\|W\|^3$ from this in closed form and checked it against the full $Q$-operator code bit-for-bit ($<10^{-15}$ agreement) for $6\le n\le9$, all $p$. The resulting normalized value matches the **Tachibana-trick section's** formula $(P/\|W\|^3)^2=2(n-1)(n-2)/n^2$ at the balanced split *exactly*, e.g. $n=8$: $1.145644$ both ways. A direct sweep over all integer splits $2\le p\le n-2$ for $n=6,\dots,30$ confirms **the balanced split ($p=q$, or $|p-q|=1$ for odd $n$) uniquely maximizes $P$ among two-factor sphere products at every $n$ tested**, no skewed split ever wins, consistent with (and now triple-checked against) the "Nonassociative algebra" section's Step 2.

**2. More than two sphere factors is always strictly worse.** Extended the diagonal block formula to $m$-block products $S^{n_1}\times\cdots\times S^{n_m}$ ($\sum n_i=n$, each $n_i\ge2$) and swept all partitions for $m=2,3,4$ at $n=8,\dots,24$. Result: **best 3-block $<$ best 2-block, and best 4-block $<$ best 3-block, at every $n$ tested**, by a wide margin (e.g. $n=12$: 2-block $(6,6)\to1.2360$, 3-block best $(2,5,5)\to1.0168$, 4-block best $(2,2,2,6)\to0.8408$). Moreover the optimal $m\ge3$-block split always degenerates toward the boundary, extra blocks get pushed to the minimum size $2$ rather than balancing (e.g. best 3-block is always $(2,k,k)$, never balanced three-way), i.e. splitting curvature across more than two factors is monotonically self-defeating, not merely suboptimal at the balanced point. **This rules out triple (and higher) sphere products as competitors for all $n$ tested, with high confidence** (exact diagonal-formula arithmetic, no approximation).

**3. The naive "$\mathbb{CP}^2$ zero-padded into $\mathbb{R}^n$" is critical only at $n=4,5$, an important precision on what the literature's competitor actually is.** Built the complex-space-form curvature $4$-tensor explicitly ($T_{ijkl}=(\delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}-\delta_{il}\delta_{jk})+(J_{ik}J_{jl}-J_{il}J_{jk})+2J_{ij}J_{kl}$ on a fixed $4$-plane $V\subset\mathbb R^n$ with orthogonal complex structure $J$, zero outside $V$), verified it satisfies the first Bianchi identity exactly and has $\mathrm{Ric}=2(m+1)g=6g$ on $V$ ($m=2$, matching the textbook Fubini–Study normalization of holomorphic sectional curvature $4$, a hard, independent geometric check that passed exactly). Weyl-projected this (using the general, non-diagonal $n$-dimensional Weyl formula) and tested idempotency $Q(\hat W)\propto\hat W$: **exact idempotency ($<10^{-15}$ relative residual) at $n=4,5$ only; for $n=6,7,8$ the relative residual $\|Q(\hat W)-\lambda\hat W\|/\|Q(\hat W)\|$ is $0.225$, $0.241$, $0.228$ respectively, definitively not a critical point.** So the literal "take $\mathbb{CP}^2$'s Weyl tensor and zero-pad it into $\mathbb{R}^n$" construction, taken at face value, is **not** the critical point responsible for the $n=8$–$11$ counterexample; something else must be meant.

**4. The actual persistent competitor, found directly, and an exact third confirmation of the $n=6+2\sqrt7$ crossover.** Solving explicitly for which linear combination $s\cdot(\text{round-sphere pattern on }V) + t\cdot(\text{pure }J\text{-correction})$ (restricted to $V$, zero outside, the unique $2$-parameter family compatible with Bianchi, confirmed by computing the rank of the Bianchi-constraint matrix directly: rank $1$ out of $3$ coefficients, so a $2$-dimensional solution space) stays idempotent for all $n$, found a **clean, closed-form answer**: the specific ratio $s{:}t=1{:}{-1}$ is *already Ricci-flat identically* ($\mathrm{Ric}\equiv0$ on $V$, computed exactly, not just numerically small), hence it equals its own Weyl tensor with no projection needed, and (since $R^\#$ of a tensor supported on $V$ with zero outside cannot see the extra ambient dimensions at all, every bracket term touching the complement multiplies a zero entry of the tensor) **this specific tensor is exactly idempotent for every $n\ge4$, verified directly for $n=4,\dots,12$, all to $<10^{-15}$ relative residual, with an identical $P$-value at every single $n$:**
$$P/\|W\|^3 = -\sqrt{3/2}\approx-1.224745 \quad (\text{sign-corrected: } +\sqrt{3/2}, \text{ using } Q(-W)=Q(W) \Rightarrow -W \text{ also critical with } P(-W)=-P(W)).$$
This construction is precisely $\mathbb{CP}^2$-type in the sense of being built from the same ingredients (round-sphere pattern $+$ orthogonal complex structure on a fixed $4$-plane, zero outside), but with the coefficient ratio fixed by *automatic Ricci-flatness* rather than by matching genuine positive Fubini–Study curvature, i.e. it is almost certainly the same object as **Fox's $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)$** (Lemma L10.1, "Nonassociative algebra" section above), reconstructed here from a completely independent starting point (explicit curvature tensor + numerical Weyl/$Q$ machinery, no Fox paper used). Comparing $+\sqrt{3/2}$ against the balanced sphere-product value $\sqrt{2(n-1)(n-2)/n^2}$ (same convention, cross-validated in Step 1 above) gives the crossover equation $2(n-1)(n-2)/n^2=3/2\iff n^2-12n+8=0\iff n=6\pm2\sqrt7$, **the identical equation, and identical crossover $n\approx11.2915$, found by the "Nonassociative algebra" section via Fox's abstract algebra**, this time from raw coordinates. (The two derivations' absolute values differ by a uniform, convention-only factor, mine is exactly $2\times$ Fox's $P$ i.e. $4\times$ in $P^2$, consistent with Fox's own noted $\tfrac16$-scalar-convention caveat combined with an inner-product normalization difference on $S^2(\Lambda^2V)$ vs. operator-on-$\Lambda^2$, but the crossover *ratio*, which is all that matters for comparing competitors, is exactly convention-independent and matches to machine precision.) **This is now a triply-independent confirmation (Fox-algebra, second-variation-adjacent coordinate computation, and this direct construction) of $n=6+2\sqrt7\approx11.29$ as the exact crossover, with $n\ge12$ the sharp integer threshold.**

**5. A different, also-genuine but non-competitive $\mathbb{CP}^2\times S^{n-4}$ critical point.** Separately, forcing the complement block $\mathbb{R}^{n-4}$ to carry round-sphere curvature $\kappa=6/(q-1)$ ($q=n-4$, chosen to match the $\mathbb{CP}^2$ block's Einstein constant $6$) gives a *different* exactly-idempotent tensor (Einstein product $\mathbb{CP}^2\times S^{n-4}$, verified idempotent to machine precision for $n=6,\dots,10$), but its $P$-value ($0.76$ at $n=6$ rising slowly to $0.85$ at $n=10$) is far **below** both the sphere-product and the point-4 competitor throughout, and a $1$-parameter scan of the complement curvature $a$ (with $\mathbb{CP}^2$ block fixed) shows this Einstein point sits at a **local minimum** of $P$ along that slice, not a maximum. **This family is cleanly ruled out as a competitor**, and illustrates that not every idempotent built from plausible-looking symmetric-space ingredients is relevant, only the specific Ricci-flat one in point 4 is.

**Confidence.** High for points 1, 2, and 3 (direct, validated arithmetic/numerics, cross-checked against two other independently-written sections). High for the qualitative finding in point 4 (the exact idempotency and $n$-independence are machine-precision facts, not fits) and for the crossover match itself (same equation obtained two independent ways). Moderate for the precise identification of the point-4 tensor with Fox's $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)$ specifically (plausible and consistent in every checkable respect. Ricci-flatness, $n$-independence, exact crossover match, but the algebraic dictionary between the two constructions was not written out term-by-term). Moderate-high for point 5's negative conclusion (Einstein-product family ruled out), the local-min finding rests on a $1$-parameter slice scan, not a full ambient Hessian.

### Vectorized Hessian computation

The Hessian quadratic form $\Phi(H):=\langle W_{\text{unit}},Q(H)\rangle$ is exactly quadratic in $H$, hence equals $\mathrm{vec}(H)^\top Q_{\text{form}}\,\mathrm{vec}(H)$ for a single fixed symmetric matrix $Q_{\text{form}}$ built once from the $\mathfrak{so}(n)$ structure constants and $W^*$'s diagonal entries. This turns the full tangent-space Hessian into one matrix product, $M=E_{\text{tan}}\,Q_{\text{form}}\,E_{\text{tan}}^\top$ ($E_{\text{tan}}$ the flattened orthonormal tangent basis), rather than $O(D_t^2)$ individual pairwise evaluations. [scripts/hessian_fast.py](scripts/lib/hessian_fast.py) implements this on top of the same trusted primitives as [scripts/hessian_pipeline_b.py](scripts/lib/hessian_pipeline_b.py)/[scripts/rsharp_basis_free.py](scripts/lib/rsharp_basis_free.py) (same Bianchi/Ricci setup, same structure constants, same Hessian coefficient $6M-3\lambda I$), verified bit-for-bit against it across six $(n,p,q)$ cases spanning $n=6$–$11$, both balanced and unbalanced. This is the script that generated the table in "Second-variation Hessian attempt" above, including its $n=12$ row (4.3 seconds total, vs. minutes for the direct double loop).

**Confidence.** High, a provably exact reformulation of the same quadratic form, not an approximation, cross-checked bit-for-bit before use on new cases.

### Explicit hypercomplex construction and cross-check

**Purpose.** Two things, using Pipeline C's explicit-tensor machinery ([curvature_operator.py](scripts/lib/curvature_operator.py), [weyl_decomposition.py](scripts/lib/weyl_decomposition.py)), independent of Fox's abstract algebra except for using his stated formulas as a target to reconstruct literally: (1) close the "algebraic dictionary not written out term-by-term" gap flagged in the "Competitor elimination" section between Fox's $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ and this repo's independently-found Ricci-flat competitor; (2) build actual hypercomplex-structure curvature tensors as an independent numerical cross-check of the "Hyper-Kähler subalgebra idempotent classification" section above, which used Fox's abstract Jordan-algebra machinery.

**Part 1, exact identification, term by term.** Fetched arXiv:1901.04012 and read Section 6 (products $\star$ and $\cdot$) and Lemma L10.1 directly from `pdftotext -layout` output. Fox's index formulas are $(g\star g)_{ijkl}=g_{k[i}g_{j]l}-g_{l[i}g_{j]k}$ (his (6.1), for symmetric tensors) and $(\alpha\cdot\beta)_{ijkl}=-3\big(\alpha_{k[i}\beta_{j]l}-\alpha_{l[i}\beta_{j]k}-2\alpha_{[ij}\beta_{kl]}\big)$ (his (6.2), for 2-forms), with $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)=\tfrac1{r+2}\big(\tfrac3{r-1}g\star g-\alpha\cdot\alpha\big)$ (his (10.2)). Implemented these literally in [run_fox_S4_check.py](scripts/lib/run_fox_S4_check.py): the $[i,j]$-antisymmetrization brackets and the full 4-index antisymmetrization $\alpha_{[ij}\beta_{kl]}$ are both computed by brute-force permutation sums (`itertools.permutations`, with sign tracked by explicit cycle decomposition), not by hand-simplified index algebra, specifically to remove sign/combinatorial-factor risk. Built $g$ = projection onto a fixed 4-plane and $\alpha$ = the fundamental 2-form of the complex structure $J$ used in [cp2_tensor.py](scripts/lib/cp2_tensor.py)'s `build_J`, then formed $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ literally with $r=4$.

**Result: exact match, not approximate.** Comparing this literal construction entrywise against [run_cp2_ricci_flat.py](scripts/lib/run_cp2_ricci_flat.py)'s $(s,t)=(1,-1)$ Ricci-flat tensor (the "Competitor elimination" section's independently-found competitor) gives $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)_{\text{Fox literal}} = \tfrac16\cdot T_{s=1,t=-1}$ with relative residual **exactly $0.0$** (not just machine epsilon, literal floating-point zero), checked at $n=4,5,6,8,10$. So the two constructions are the *same tensor* up to the scalar $1/6$, which is precisely Fox's own $\tfrac1{r+2}=\tfrac16$ prefactor in (10.2), i.e. `run_cp2_ricci_flat.py`'s tensor is exactly $(r+2)\cdot\mathcal S^4(\alpha)=6\,\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$, term for term. Additional cross-checks all passed exactly: the literal Fox tensor has `max|Ricci|=0.0` (not approximately zero. Fox's item (1), $\mathcal S^r(\alpha)\in\mathcal{MC}_{\mathcal W}$, verified exactly), is a machine-precision eigenvector of Pipeline C's own $Q$ operator (reldiff $9.6\times10^{-17}$), and gives $P/\|W\|^3=-\sqrt{3/2}$ (the same value already recorded, up to the documented sign convention, see below). This **fully closes the identification gap**: the "almost certainly" in the earlier section can be upgraded to "exactly, verified term-by-term from Fox's own index formulas."

**A precise account of the sign convention.** Pipeline C's raw $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ satisfies $Q_{\text{pipeline}}(\mathcal S^4(\alpha))=-1\cdot\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ exactly (eigenvalue $-1$, not $+1$), whereas Fox's normalization requires $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)*_{\text{Fox}}\mathcal S^4(\alpha)=+1\cdot\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$. This means Pipeline C's own bilinear form $B_{\text{pipeline}}(X,Y)=\tfrac12[Q(X+Y)-Q(X)-Q(Y)]$ equals $-1\times$ Fox's $*$ product uniformly (confirmed on multiple pairs in Part 2 below, not just the diagonal case), a fixed, tensor-independent sign flip, not a discrepancy. This is exactly the same sign artifact already flagged in the "Competitor elimination" section ("sign-corrected: $+\sqrt{3/2}$, using $Q(-W)=Q(W)$").

**Part 2, hypercomplex structure, algebra relations, and idempotent classification, checked numerically.** Built $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ as the fundamental 2-forms of quaternion left-multiplication-by-$i,j,k$ endomorphisms of a fixed $\mathbb R^4\subset\mathbb R^n$ (explicit $4\times4$ matrices), verified $i^2=j^2=k^2=-\mathrm{Id}$, $ij=k$, $ij=-ji$, etc. to **exact floating-point zero**. Built $\mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta),\mathcal S^4(\gamma)$ via the term-by-term-validated Fox construction from Part 1, plus the cross terms $\alpha\cdot\beta,\beta\cdot\gamma,\gamma\cdot\alpha$ via the same brute-force-antisymmetrized `dot_product_2forms` formula. All in [run_cp2_quaternion.py](scripts/runs/run_cp2_quaternion.py). Findings, all to exact-zero or machine-precision residual:

Converting via the established $-1$ sign convention, this is $-1\times$ Fox's stated relation $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)*\mathcal S^4(\beta)=-\tfrac16(\mathcal S^4(\alpha)+\mathcal S^4(\beta)-5\mathcal S^4(\gamma))=-(\mathcal S^4(\alpha)+\mathcal S^4(\beta))$ (using $\mathcal S^4(\gamma)=-\mathcal S^4(\alpha)-\mathcal S^4(\beta)$), **exact agreement** with Fox's (10.16)/(10.19), and additional confirmation that the same universal $-1$ sign factor found for the single-tensor eigenvalue also governs the full bilinear product, not just the diagonal case.

A generic off-diagonal test point of the full 5-dimensional $\mathbb B$ (mixing in $\alpha\cdot\beta,\beta\cdot\gamma$) gives a large idempotency residual ($0.96$), confirming it is not close to a critical point either.

**Agreement with the parallel "Hyper-Kähler subalgebra idempotent classification" section.** That section, working entirely from Fox's abstract Jordan-algebra isomorphism $\Psi:\mathbb B\to(\mathrm{Sym}_0(U),\times)$ (Lemma L10.8(2)), derived that every nontrivial idempotent of the rank-3 deunitalized Jordan algebra has eigenvalue pattern $(2,-1,-1)$ up to permutation, forming a single orbit through $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$, with the $120°$/$\cos=-1/2$ angle between any two of $\mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta),\mathcal S^4(\gamma)$ as a cross-check. **This is in exact agreement with the present, fully independent numerical finding**: Pipeline C's own direct eigen-ray search inside $\mathrm{Span}\{\mathcal S^4(\alpha),\mathcal S^4(\beta)\}$ (which, by the $SO(3)$-conjugation argument both sections rely on, is a complete slice of the 5-dimensional algebra up to symmetry) finds *only* the same three rays and nothing else, and the Gram-matrix angle computed here ($-0.5$ exactly) matches their $120°$ cross-check exactly. Both approaches, one abstract-algebraic, one raw-numerical on explicit curvature 4-tensors, converge on the same conclusion: **$\mathbb B$'s only nontrivial idempotents are hyper-Kähler-rotated copies of $\mathcal S^4(\alpha)$ itself, all with $P/\|W\|^3=\sqrt{3/2}$, so $\mathbb B$ contributes no new competitor.** As a corollary made explicit here: the task's "natural symmetric combination" $(\mathcal S^4(\alpha)+\mathcal S^4(\beta)+\mathcal S^4(\gamma))/\sqrt3$ is **identically zero** (confirmed to exact floating-point $0.0$), not merely suboptimal, it is not a valid unit-norm competitor at all, which is itself the numerical manifestation of Fox's Lemma 10.7(4a).

**Confidence.** High for Part 1 (the entrywise match is exact floating-point zero at multiple $n$, not a numerical approximation, and both the antisymmetrization brackets and the star/dot product formulas were implemented mechanically from Fox's stated index formulas via brute-force permutation sums, removing hand-algebra sign risk).
